subject: Data type treating column and row ID variables symmetrically?

messages.author: 26ca10a1ecf81e72
messages.subject: Data type treating column and row ID variables symmetrically?
parts:
Hello Everyone!

Does anybody knows of an data type and manipulation facilities for data tables
with multiple column variables as in the following example:

| | | a | a | a | b | b | <- cv1
| | | c | c | d | d | e | <- cv2
|-----+-----+---+---+---+---+---|
| x | v | 5 | 5 | 1 | 1 | 2 |
| x | W | 8 | 5 | 0 | 1 | 7 |
| y | v | 5 | 2 | 6 | 1 | 2 |
| z | v | 6 | 9 | 1 | 9 | 7 |
| z | W | 0 | 0 | 7 | 6 | 6 |
^ ^
rv1 rv3

Here cv1 and cv2 are column ID variables (vary by column).

Row ID variables are rv1 and rv2 (vary by rows).

Data.frame is limited in this respect, it does not distinguish between
row/column ID variables' names and allow only for one column variable.

Reshape package overcomes partially this problem by pasting the column variables
(cv1, cv2) into one with "_" separator.

So to be more precise, what would be the easiest strategy to
(1) import such data, and
(2) reshape it into the long form?

Preferably an automated tool designed specifically to this type of problems. Does
exist any? Reshape comes close but still requires quite some computation.

(3) Also an export tool to the rectangular format as above? It's many times useful
to present your data in a user-friendly way.

Many thanks for any suggestions,
Vitally.

Hi:

After a little trial and error, I came up with this:

# Attempt to use read.ftable():

# File prep:
Input file (pipes stripped, column labels quoted, some other stuff, per example(read.ftable):
[tedious!]

"           \'a\'  \'a\'  \'a\'  \'b\'  \'b\' \n",  
"           \'c\'  \'c\'  \'d\'  \'d\'  \'e\' \n",  
" x    v    5  5  1  1  2 \n",
" x    W    8  5  0  1  7 \n",
" y    v    5  2  6  1  2 \n",
" z    v    6  9  1  9  7 \n",
" z    W    0  0  7  6  6 \n",

(By the way, why do you have two columns labeled 'a c'?
Shouldn't they be merged, or is the second meant to be 'b c' ?)

# R code:

temp <- tempfile()
cat("           \'a\'  \'a\'  \'a\'  \'b\'  \'b\' \n",  
"           \'c\'  \'c\'  \'d\'  \'d\'  \'e\' \n",  
" x    v    5  5  1  1  2 \n",
" x    W    8  5  0  1  7 \n",
" y    v    5  2  6  1  2 \n",
" z    v    6  9  1  9  7 \n",
" z    W    0  0  7  6  6 \n", file = temp)
file.show(temp)
ft <- read.ftable(temp, skip = 2, row.var.names = list(c('F1', 'F2')),
            col.vars = list('F3' = c('a', 'b'),
                            'F4' = c('c', 'd', 'e')))
Warning message:
In read.ftable(temp, skip = 2, row.var.names = list(c("F1", "F2")),  :
  NAs introduced by coercion
> ft
              F3  a        b     
              F4  c  d  e  c  d  e
c("F1", "F2")                    
'x'              NA  5  5  1  1  2
'y'              NA  8  5  0  1  7
'z'              NA  5  2  6  1  2

Not quite - it seems that three variables is the limit for read.ftable(). (Things weren't any different when I used
row.var.names = c('F1', 'F2') other than a second column of c('x', 'x', 'x').)

Back to the drawing board - this time we create a data frame and build an ftable from that.

# Plan B:
# Make vectors of the factor levels
> f1 <- c('x', 'y', 'z')
> f2 <- c('v', 'W')
> f3 <- c('a', 'b')
> f4 <- c('c', 'd', 'e')
# Use expand.grid() to get their combinations

# I had my reasons for doing this at the time, but...
df <- expand.grid(f3 = f3, f4 = f4, f1 = f1, f2 = f2)

# Now create the vector of frequencies that correspond to these particular combinations:
df$v <- c(5, 5, 1, 1, NA, 2, 5, 2, 6, 1, NA, 2, 6, 9, 1, 9, NA, 7,
           8, 5, 0, 1, NA, 7, rep(NA, 6), 0, 0, 7, 6, NA, 6)

# Use xtabs() to create a 4-way table:

tab1 <- xtabs(v ~ ., data = df)

# Make the flat table:
ftable(tab1, row.vars = c(3, 4))
      f3 a     b   
      f4 c d e c d e
f1 f2              
x  v     5 1 0 5 1 2
   W     8 0 0 5 1 7
y  v     5 6 0 2 1 2
   W     0 0 0 0 0 0
z  v     6 1 0 9 9 7
   W     0 7 0 0 6 6

Now you know why it's easier to read a flat file into a statistical program than a flat table, and have something tangible to take to your colleagues for future reference.

HTH,
Dennis

If they are not numeric, what are they? Character? If so, they can be coerced to numeric after the file is processed into a more suitable form for statistical analysis.

I am a bit surprise that the features I asked about are not demanded.
Every now and then guys are coming to me with excell sheets with the
data in a rectangular form.

You have a four-dimensional table flattened into two dimensions. That's rather...unusual. The conventional way to read something like that into R would be to have a data frame-like file with four factor columns and a numeric column of frequencies. R (and every other statistical software with which I am familiar) prefer such files over flat rectangular tables. Essentially, that's what you're going to have to do if you expect to perform statistical analysis of some kind on that data.


Any further suggestions?

A concrete example data set and what you've tried and failed with would be helpful. And since this is not really about plyr or reshape(2) at this point, this should probably be moved to R-help.

Dennis

It has to do with reshape more than with anything else in this world.

Here is the example taken from reshape2 for "dcast":

names(ChickWeight) <- tolower(names(ChickWeight))
chick_m <- melt(ChickWeight, id=2:4, na.rm=TRUE)
dcast(chick_m, time ~ variable + diet, mean) # average effect of time

Here is the casted data:

time weight_1 weight_2 weight_3 weight_4
1 0 41.40000 40.7 40.8 41.0000
2 2 47.25000 49.4 50.4 51.8000
3 4 56.47368 59.8 62.2 64.5000
4 6 66.78947 75.4 77.9 83.9000

As you can see two ID variables ("variable" and "diet") are now column.variables,
but they are pasted together with "_" separator and mixed with the label
"time". "time" is an ID row.variable here.
This limitation of data.frame format is the source of all the confusion and the
reason reshape package does not have an intuitive appeal for many people.

Equivalently the data could be displayed with variables "variable" and "diet" on
separate rows:

variable weight weight weight weight
diet 1 2 3 4
time
1 0 41.40000 40.7 40.8 41.0000
2 2 47.25000 49.4 50.4 51.8000
3 4 56.47368 59.8 62.2 64.5000
4 6 66.78947 75.4 77.9 83.9000

This is strikingly similar to the format of "ftable" but it is not; ftable is
always balanced. In the rectangular representation above some levels of ID
variables could be missing.

This is the format people in the social sciences organize the experimental
data. Often the data is collected by hand, and it is easier to organize it in this
way.

So as you can see, everything is entirely in the framework of "reshape" package.

This is common requirement for me to write my own import and export functions. I
will attend to it in the near feature.

I am curious what Hadley would say about adding two attributes to casted
data.frames similar to "ftable" class:

- attr(*, "row.vars")=List of 3
- attr(*, "col.vars")=List of 1

given this information the print method could be developed for nice display of
casted data and import/export functionality easily added. Internally though it
will still be a data.frame:).

Cheers,
Vitaly.
